# Abstract: Discover and Define

Checkpoint 2. Builds on `01-current-state-audit-and-discovery-plan.md`. Still no strategy, flows or UI.

**Evidence labels.** [Fact] sourced or observed. [Hypothesis] a testable claim, no real-user evidence yet. [Synthetic] generated by me to surface questions; it is not customer evidence and must never be quoted as such. [Rec] my recommendation.

**Important:** I have no real customer research for this product. The persona, empathy map and jobs below are built from the founder's description of the ICP, from public sources cited in section 3, and from reasoning. Every one of them is a hypothesis to be broken by the real interviews.

## 2. Provisional persona (hypothesis, not a real person)

**P1: "the one who nods along".** Built from the founder's ICP: 23+ working professionals whose conversations have gone stale.

| | Hypothesis |
|---|---|
| Age and life stage | 25 to 34, 2 to 8 years into work. Single or recently partnered. [Hypothesis: the age band the community skews to, to check with event data.] |
| Work | Knowledge-work job in tech, marketing, consulting, finance or media. Long meetings, a commute or remote days. |
| City | Metro India (Abstract runs events in seven cities). Android phone as the daily device [Fact: Android is about 92 to 93 percent of Indian mobile OS share in recent StatCounter snapshots, see section 3.4]. |
| Digital routine | Phone first thing in the morning and last thing at night. Reels, YouTube, WhatsApp groups, a few newsletters or podcasts saved and mostly unread. |
| Curiosity | Used to read, watch films and argue about ideas in college. Today consumes a lot of content but retains little and retells less. |
| Motivations | Be the interesting one in a room. Stop feeling intellectually stagnant. Have a reference to bring to dinners, dates and work lunches. |
| Barriers | Tired after work. Guilt about unread reading lists. Distrust of "learning apps" that feel like homework. Skeptical of AI-generated slop. |
| Why they would return | A small, reliable moment of feeling sharper that they can use the same day with another person. |
| Why they would stop | The app feels like a chore, the content is generic, they miss a day and feel punished, or nobody notices they got cooler. |

**Segments within the ICP that I think matter (to be tested, not assumed):**
- **S1 "the performer"**: wants to impress socially (dates, parties, networking).
- **S2 "the rusty reader"**: genuinely misses curiosity, wants to feel mentally alive.
- **S3 "the community regular"**: already attends Abstract events, joins for the brand and the people.

[Rec] S3 is the fastest to reach (existing community), S1 is the clearest value moment, S2 may have the most durable habit. Interviews must tell us which one is real.

## 3. Workaround audit: what people do today

The question: when someone wants to feel more interesting or less stagnant, what do they actually do? Verdicts are about relevance to our job, not about quality.

| Workaround | What it does for them | Where it fails for this job | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short-form video (reels, shorts) | Endless trivia and facts, zero effort | Entertaining, rarely retained or retold; no structure; no verification | **Primary alternative** (the thing they would "fire") [Hypothesis] |
| Doing nothing | No cost, no guilt management | The pain stays; the avoidant default | **Primary alternative** |
| Newsletters and long reads | Depth, curation | Pile up unread; effort to start | Adjacent |
| Podcasts and YouTube explainers | Learning during commute | Passive, long, no recall prompt | Adjacent |
| Books | Depth and prestige | Time and stamina; slow payoff | Adjacent |
| Search and Wikipedia rabbit holes | On-demand answers | Pull not push; no habit; no curation | Adjacent |
| Asking a knowledgeable friend, or going to events | Social, human, memorable | Not available daily, not scalable | **Closest to our DNA** (this is what Abstract events already do) |
| Quiz and trivia apps | Fun competition | Mostly trivia for its own sake, not social usefulness | Partial |
| Microlearning apps (Knowlet, MyGrowth, Mindsnap, SmartyMe, Headway-style) | Daily short lessons, quizzes, streaks | Generic; no strong human voice; usage in India unknown | **Direct** category |
| Duolingo-style habit apps | Habit and gamification mastery | Wrong subject for this job | **Pattern source**, not a competitor |

**What the sources say, with caveats**
- [Fact] Several microlearning apps position themselves for busy adults with short daily lessons, quizzes and streaks, for example [Knowlet](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id6754519612), [MyGrowth](https://apps.apple.com/py/app/mygrowth-daily-micro-learning/id6748383002?l=en-GB), [Mindsnap](https://apps.appfollow.io/ios/mindsnap-daily-microlearning/6499518703?country=ai) and [SmartyMe](https://apppricinglab.com/app/google_play/com.app.smartyme). These are vendor store listings: marketing claims, not usage evidence. I found no India usage data.
- [Fact] Duolingo's growth write-ups credit streaks, notification changes and many small tests. One source says users with a 10-day streak dropped off less, but warns that this is correlation with selection bias, so it may not be causal. A mechanic modelled on mobile games ("limited attempts") reportedly produced no retention gain. See [this growth write-up](https://marishalakhiani.substack.com/p/breaking-down-duolingos-growth-model) and [this retention summary](https://www.strivecloud.io/blog/blog-gamification-examples-boost-user-retention-duolingo). These are secondary sources; churn figures differ between them. Do not treat any number as established.
- [Rec] Implication: a streak is a *tested-by-others hypothesis*, not a law. We should test whether it helps our users or just guilt-trips them.

**Open research needed:** actual use of short-video and microlearning apps among our ICP in India, willingness to pay for learning apps in India, and what Abstract members already do.

### 3.4 Platform fact
[Fact] StatCounter's India snapshots show Android at about 92 to 93 percent of mobile OS share and iOS about 7 to 8 percent ([StatCounter India](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-market-share/mobile-/india)). Counterpoint reports Apple's share of shipments rising to about 12 percent in Q4 2025 ([Counterpoint](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insight/global-smartphone-os-market-share)). Different measures, so not directly comparable. [Rec] Design Android-first; treat iOS as secondary until our own data says otherwise.

## 4. Empathy map for P1 (hypothesis)

| Quadrant | Hypothesis |
|---|---|
| **Think and feel** | "I used to be curious. When did I become boring?" Quiet embarrassment when a conversation moves past them. Guilt over saved articles. Wants to feel sharp, not schooled. |
| **See** | Friends who casually drop interesting references. Endless feeds of half-facts. Reading lists growing. Colleagues who seem more well-read. |
| **Hear** | "Did you read / watch / hear about…?" from friends. Pressure to be "well-rounded" in dating, work and social circles. Advice to "read more". |
| **Say and do** | Says "I'll read that later" and doesn't. Nods along. Scrolls instead of reading. Occasionally googles in the bathroom to keep up. Shares a reel as a stand-in for a thought. |
| **Pains** | Having nothing to add. Forgetting what they read. Content that is long, generic or unverified. Apps that make them feel guilty for missing a day. Being obviously "performing" knowledge. |
| **Gains** | One good story to tell tonight. Being the person people want to talk to. Feeling mentally alive. A small daily win that is visible to someone else. |

---

## 5. Jobs to be done (hypotheses)

The underlying job is not "learn". It is **"be more interesting to other people, and feel more alive myself."**

**Functional**
- J1. When I'm about to be in a social or work conversation, I want a good story or fact I can tell in under a minute, so I can contribute something that lands.
- J2. When I come across something interesting, I want it to stay with me, so I can retell it later without notes.
- J3. When I have five spare minutes, I want one worthwhile thing to do with them, so I can feel I used the time well instead of scrolling.

**Emotional**
- J4. When I feel mentally stale, I want a small daily proof that I am still curious, so I can feel sharp and proud of myself.
- J5. When I miss a day, I want to come back without guilt, so I can keep the habit without shame.

**Social**
- J6. When I'm with people I want to impress or connect with, I want to be seen as curious and well-informed, so I can be someone people enjoy talking to.
- J7. When I find something good, I want to share it with the right person, so I can feel connected through ideas.

**Triggers:** an event (dinner, date, party, meeting), the moment after being left out of a conversation, an Abstract event, a moment of boredom in a commute, a new year or new job.
**Reasons to stop:** content that feels generic or repetitive, a long or heavy session, guilt on a missed day, the product doesn't help in a real conversation, a better-looking feed appears.
**What would make Abstract worth returning to:** a clear "I used this" moment within 24 hours (J1), and a feeling of being a bit sharper than yesterday (J4).

[Rec] J1 and J6 (say it in a real conversation) are the load-bearing jobs, and the "best line to say out loud" question is the product's most original answer to them. Everything else should support those two.

## 6. Define (converge): draft, needs your confirmation

**Problem statement (draft).** Working professionals who feel their conversations have gone stale lack a low-effort, trustworthy way to collect one good story at a time and actually use it in conversation. They consume plenty, retain little, and retell almost nothing.

**Target segment (draft, decision D1).** Start with S3 (existing Abstract community members, 25 to 34) because they are reachable and already trust the brand, aiming at S1/S2 behaviour. Validate with interviews.

**Value proposition (draft).** One real story a day, picked and checked by a person, that you can retell the same day. Five minutes. You come away with a line to say out loud.

**Why Abstract, not an alternative (hypothesis).** A recognisable human curator and community behind the stories, the culturally specific voice, and an explicit "say it out loud" step, rather than another generic feed or quiz.

**What this means for the product (to be tested):**
- Success is **retelling**, not completion.
- The human must be **felt** in the content, not just stated.
- The daily habit exists to serve the retelling, not the other way round.

## 7. Synthetic interviews (NOT customer evidence)

> **Synthetic.** I wrote these to rehearse the guide and expose objections. They are fictional, generated from my assumptions, and contain no real quotes or data. They must not appear in any report as findings.

**Synthetic A: "performer" (30, product manager, Bengaluru).**
Likely objection: "I already get facts from reels; why pay attention to another app?"
Surfaces: how do we beat reels for attention? What does *more interesting* mean to them? Do they remember the reel facts a week later?

**Synthetic B: "rusty reader" (28, consultant, Mumbai).**
Likely objection: "I'll feel guilty when I miss a day, so I'll avoid starting."
Surfaces: how do they feel about streaks? Is guilt or pride the stronger force?

**Synthetic C: "community regular" (32, marketing, Delhi).**
Likely objection: "I like Abstract events because of the people. An app feels impersonal."
Surfaces: does the human curator matter? Would they come back for the community, the content or the friends?

**Questions these raised for the real interviews:** reels vs us; guilt vs pride about streaks; whether the human voice matters; whether "retelling" is a real behaviour; where weekends sit in their routine.

## 8. Real interview guide (45 minutes)

**Recruiting.** 10 to 12 people from the Abstract community: 25 to 35, working, mix of cities, mix of event attendance (regulars and one-time), at least 3 who have never attended. Do not interview friends of the team.

**Consent.** Say what it's for, that it is recorded or noted, that nothing they say is attributed, that they can skip any question. No incentives that bias answers beyond a small thank-you.

**Rules.** Ask about the past, not the future. Do not pitch. Do not ask "would you use this?" Ask for specific recent examples.

| # | Question | What we learn |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tell me about the last time you were in a conversation and wished you had something to add. | The trigger, the feeling, the frequency (J1, J4) |
| 2 | What did you do about it, in the moment and afterwards? | Real workarounds |
| 3 | Where did you last learn something interesting? How did you find it? | Channels (workaround audit) |
| 4 | What did you do with it afterwards? Did you tell anyone? | Retelling behaviour (H3) |
| 5 | Walk me through a typical weekday from waking up. Where are the gaps? | Habit moments (H5) |
| 6 | And a Saturday or Sunday? | Weekend behaviour (A7) |
| 7 | Have you tried any app to learn or stay curious? What happened? Why did you stop? | Why habit apps fail for them |
| 8 | Have you ever kept a streak of anything? How did it feel when it broke? | Pride vs guilt |
| 9 | Show them two versions of a daily item (with and without a short note from a named person). Which would you trust more, and why? | Human-curation value (A6) |
| 10 | Tell me about Abstract: what do you remember, what do you associate with it? | Brand and community pull (A3) |
| 11 | If something helped you be more interesting, what would you give up for it: time, money, attention? | Willingness to trade |
| 12 | Who else would you tell about it? When? | Referral moments |

**After each interview (30 minutes).** Capture: top 3 quotes with context, the trigger, the workaround, the emotion, a surprise. Never write summaries that blend interviews.

**Synthesis (after 10 to 12).** Cluster by job, not by person. Count how many people show each behaviour. Report the count, not the conclusion: "7 of 11 retold nothing", not "people don't retell".

**Kill criteria (set before, as hypotheses, calibrate later).** If fewer than about a third describe a recurring felt gap, or if most already have a retelling habit, stop and rethink the problem before building more.

## 9. Behavioural principles: verification notes

You asked me to verify names before applying them.

| Principle | Verified meaning | Relevance to a concrete decision |
|---|---|---|
| **Jakob's Law** | Users expect your product to work like others they already know ([Laws of UX](https://lawsofux.com/index.md)). | Swipe cards, a quiz bar and bottom feedback sheet should match familiar patterns; phone or Google sign-in over email links. |
| **Fitts's Law** | Time to hit a target depends on its size and distance. | Primary action at the bottom within thumb reach, large targets, the "next" button never moves. |
| **Von Restorff effect** | The item that differs from the rest is remembered. | The "say it out loud" card is the only yellow card; the curator note is visually distinct. |
| **Peak-end rule** | People judge an experience mostly by its high point and its end. | Design the end of every session: the line to say, then a human sign-off, not a score. |
| **Goal-gradient and Zeigarnik** | Motivation rises as a goal nears; unfinished tasks stick in memory. | Visible progress through the story; a half-finished story is easy to resume. |
| **Gruen effect** | **I read this as the "Gruen transfer":** shoppers in a deliberately disorienting layout lose track of their purpose and buy on impulse ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruen_transfer), noted as needing better sourcing). | **A warning, not a tool.** We should not disorient users to push purchases or time. If you meant something else, tell me. |
| **"Perkins' Law"** | I could not verify any such UX law. **My best guess is Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_law)). | A hard five-minute ceiling keeps the session from bloating. If you meant something else, tell me. |

Nielsen's ten heuristics will be applied against the actual flows in the next checkpoint, where they can be checked screen by screen.
